summary: Adversarial debate and scoring of skill-taxonomy variants V1-V5 (+V2-lite)

advocates.strongest_case: The audit's stack-specificity table is the decisive fact: solidstats-backend-ts-conventions carries 16 ts-shared sections against 3 universal and 8 stack-specific — the extraction pressure in this corpus is TypeScript-shaped, not doctrine-shaped. The ~400-line band shared by server-2 and replays-fetcher (naming/factories, typed-error base, const-union enums, config discipline, async safety, external adapters, §Z/§AA/§AB) is written in ESLint-enforced, es-toolkit/day.js/nanoid idiom that a Rust crate literally cannot consume, so the correct audience for the shared layer is exactly "the two TS services" — which is what V1 names: solidstats-process-backend-ts-standards. The trigger question that started this debate dies by name construction: the parser is excluded because the name says "ts", ending the "name says yes, content says no" failure without inventing a doctrine tier. Migration is the cheapest of any structural variant: the draft solidstats-process-backend-standards already exists on disk (SKILL.md, 173 lines, plus references/correctness-and-quality.md, already requiring ts-standards) — V1 is a rename plus the two content moves every variant needs anyway: utilities and TS test idioms up to process-ts-standards, which fixes confirmed duplications #1 and #5 (the db37f07 double-add of es-toolkit/type-fest/day.js/nanoid to both backend and frontend conventions, and the typed-builders/test.each/@ts-expect-error/fake-timers idioms stranded in backend-ts-tests). On enforceability — judge criterion 8 — V1 is structurally superior: every rule lives at idiom level, so backend-ts-code-review cites pino-field §Z gates directly, and parser-rust-code-review cites a Rust-native observability section (tracing spans, Drop/RAII, bounded channels) added as one more reference in the spine+references layout parser-rust-conventions already uses (worker-build-perf.md, determinism-and-contract.md, parsing-types-errors.md, per f283fa0). The Rust gap closes with real translation done once, in its natural home — the same translation work the taxonomy doc admits V2 forces anyway, because "a doctrine skill alone is not enforceable, so every rule ends up written twice". Token cost is roughly net-zero despite the nominally 4-deep chain: process-backend-ts-standards content replaces what would otherwise sit inside both repo skills, and no rule is read twice per task. Fetcher's confirmed real stack (pino, zod 4, pg, @aws-sdk/client-s3, p-limit, commander, no HTTP framework) gets its own trio, while the genuinely shared band — none of it Fastify-shaped — lives above, ending the under-described "shared baseline" note in backend-ts-conventions. Against V5, the nearest competitor: V1's own tree already includes everything structural in V5 (utilities + TS test idioms in ts-standards, the fetcher trio, the Rust observability section); V5's only true additions are an AGENTS naming sentence — a hygiene line any winner should get during the migration that must touch all four out-of-sync AGENTS tables anyway — and a parity-by-note contract the doc itself concedes is "weaker than parity-by-file", in a family that has no review-feedback learning loop (audit gap #4) to police such notes. V1 states the TS/Rust two-forms drift risk honestly in its con list instead of papering it over with an unenforced promise that reviewers will wrongly trust. It is the smallest-churn, fully idiom-enforceable, honestly-named taxonomy that fixes both confirmed duplications, closes the Rust observability gap, and keeps every process- skill a true meta layer in line with the estesis pattern the family copied.

attacks.attack: A developer adds a new lapin consumer to parser-worker and the reviewer must enforce the external-adapter taxonomy. process-service-standards has no code samples by design, so the Rust evidence gate (what a compliant tracing span / bounded channel / shutdown handler looks like) must live in parser-rust-conventions anyway — the agent reads doctrine + Rust translation + repo skill, and the doctrine read bought nothing but tokens. When §AB resource lifecycle gains a fourth leg, the edit fans out to doctrine + TS gate + Rust gate (3+ files) versus V1's 2 — worse update ergonomics, the exact criterion V2 claims to win. Worse, replay-parser-2 is a 5-crate workspace where parser-cli, parser-core, and parser-quality are not service-shaped at all; binding the whole repo to service doctrine means every deterministic-parsing task in parser-core pays a +1 read for graceful-shutdown and adapter taxonomy it cannot use. The precedent V2 leans on (review/testing standards working cross-stack) holds only because review behavior is genuinely stack-free — code idiom is not, as the audit's 16-ts-shared-sections finding proves.

V2-lite adds a hard-require read for every stack including web — a pre-code planning stub with no src/ — so every future React component task reads project-standards + ts-standards + code-standards + frontend-react-conventions to inherit 'resource-lifecycle three-legs' doctrine that a component barely touches. The fourth process- skill must also be added to GSD:skills tables in all four repos, which the audit shows are already out of sync in all four (parser missing project-standards; everyone missing ts-standards) — one more table row to drift. And the surgery is bloody: the audit says only the code-quality bug list's *portable half* moves, so one checklist gets split into a portable half (code-standards) and a TS half (backend-ts-standards); a reviewer enforcing the bug list now consults two skills, and the halves will disagree the first time someone patches one — the same failure mode already CHANGELOG-recorded for the backend reviewer's severity table. Pulling the 6 universal sections out of a draft that interleaves them with 11 ts-shared sections also orphans cross-references inside the remaining 11.

V3 institutionalizes the pattern that is already producing audit findings: commit db37f07 added the same utilities guidance to two conventions files in one commit, and it is now duplication finding #1. Scale that to the full ~400-line band: when the typed-error base rule changes (say, error-code naming), the editor patches backend-ts-conventions and forgets fetcher-ts-conventions; backend-ts-code-review and the fetcher reviewer now enforce contradictory gates, and a fetcher MR gets flagged for following the newer server-2 rule. The audit already documents this exact failure in miniature — the backend reviewer's severity table is 'a known second source of truth' with a CHANGELOG-recorded unsatisfiable-instruction fix. V3 also directly contradicts the repo's own 'absorb once, single source' authoring standard in AGENTS.md, so the first /skill-creator pass over the duplicated fetcher skill will try to re-extract the shared layer V3 just killed.

V4 renames 9+ skills, which breaks install keys in skills-lock.json, GSD:skills tables in all four repos, README, and every consumer's memory — in a corpus where the audit shows those AGENTS tables are *already* missing locked skills in all four repos today. Concrete mid-migration failure: server-2's AGENTS table still lists solidstats-backend-ts-conventions while the lock holds solidstats-server2-ts-conventions; the agent's lookup misses, and a new module ships without layers.md's Fastify/TypeBox/Kysely rules — silent rule loss during the riskiest window, multiplied across 9 renames and 4 repos. The payoff over V1 plus one AGENTS sentence is purely cosmetic: the 'backend' ambiguity dies either way once the naming rule is written down. And 'server2' as a scope token is fragile — a repo literally named server-2 implies a server-3; tying skill names to repo names imports repo churn into the taxonomy.

V5 is V1 wearing extra promises. Structurally it adds nothing: V1's tree already moves utilities and TS test idioms to process-ts-standards, creates the fetcher trio, and closes the Rust gap inside parser-rust-conventions. V5's two genuine additions are an AGENTS naming sentence — a migration hygiene line, not a taxonomy — and the parity-by-note contract, which its own write-up concedes is 'weaker than parity-by-file — it relies on review discipline' in a family the audit says lacks any review-feedback learning loop (gap #4) to police it. Concrete failure: §Z in process-backend-ts-standards gains a no-PII-in-log-fields rule; nothing mechanically touches the parser mirror; six months later parser-rust-code-review approves a worker change logging player identifiers because its mirrored section predates the rule — and because the header *claims* parity, the reviewer trusts it, which is strictly worse than V1's honest 'two written forms that can drift' con. Picking V5 over V1 means scoring an unenforced promise as a drift mechanism (judge criterion 3) when it is a comment.

own_weaknesses: Drift between the two written forms of §Z/§AA/§AB (TS in process-backend-ts-standards, Rust in parser-rust-conventions) has no mechanism at all in V1 — not even V5's note. When the TS form changes, nothing hints a Rust mirror exists; divergence is detected only if a human remembers.

The 'backend' word still does double duty: backend-ts-conventions scopes to server-2 only while process-backend-ts-standards scopes to both TS services. Without an explicit AGENTS sentence (which V1 does not mandate), the original trigger confusion recurs one level down — e.g. an agent on a replays-fetcher task reads backend-ts-conventions by name and applies Fastify/TypeBox/Kysely rules to a commander/pg/p-limit CLI.

Read chain for any TS-service task is 4 deep (project-standards → ts-standards → backend-ts-standards → repo trio). For a trivial one-file fetcher fix, V1 has the worst tokens-per-task of all variants except V2; V3 beats it on chain depth for small tasks.

The six genuinely language-agnostic sections the audit found (SOLID thresholds, DRY rule-of-three, comments policy, portable bug-list half, resource three-legs, swallowed-error principle) stay buried inside a TS-services skill. Parser and web inherit none of them; when web's frontend-react-conventions matures past the pre-code stub, those sections will be re-stated there — a future duplication V2-lite prevents by design.

The 'two TS services' audience is contingent: the fetcher tree already carries an 'architecture when converged' note, and any third TS service (or fetcher converging on server-2's module layout) forces re-litigating what process-backend-ts-standards means.

advocates.strongest_case: The trigger question — "should the Rust parser depend on backend-standards?" — is only answered cleanly by V2, because the corpus shows the parser worker IS the third service in every operational sense: replay-parser-2's parser-worker crate runs tokio + lapin + aws-sdk-s3 + tracing, i.e. a queue consumer with S3 adapters, shutdown, and observability concerns identical in kind to server-2 (infra/, operations/, queue) and replays-fetcher (whose src literally has errors/, logging/, checkpoint/, storage/, staging/ — §Z/§AA/§AB-shaped capability dirs). V1/V5 answer "no, by name construction," which leaves the one repo with a CONFIRMED doctrine gap (corpus-audit Gaps #1: no log-hygiene/diagnosability/resource doctrine in parser-rust-conventions, only a tracing mention in worker-build-perf-adjacent content) outside the only layer that carries that doctrine; V2 closes the gap by force, because the doctrine binds the worker and the Rust idiom gate must be written to satisfy it. The audit measured the doctrine fuel: the parked draft (solidstats-process-backend-standards) carries 6 sections judged genuinely language-agnostic, and the service-shaped list (error taxonomy, §Z/§AA observability, §AB lifecycle, config fail-fast, adapter taxonomy, graceful shutdown) is behavior-level content — exactly the class that already works cross-stack in this corpus: process-testing-standards is 12/12 universal sections and process-review-standards 7/8, both binding Rust and React today with zero drift incidents. So the "doctrine skills don't work for code" objection is refuted by two live counterexamples in the same family. The decisive criterion is #3, drift mechanism, because this corpus has three documented note/delegation failures: the "fetcher baseline" note in backend-ts-conventions that the audit says "under-describes the mismatch" (fetcher is pino/zod4/pg/commander, not Fastify); frontend-react-conventions/typescript.md restating no-any/no-interface "despite delegation note"; and the backend-ts-code-review severity table, a known second source of truth with a CHANGELOG-recorded drift fix. Every rival variant's anti-drift story is some flavor of the mechanism that already failed three times (V5's "mirrors §Z/§AA/§AB — keep in sync" one-liner, V3's review vigilance over ~400 duplicated lines, V1's nothing at all); V2's mechanism is a shared file — the only mechanism with a working precedent here. V2 also fixes review-skill coherence: today the audit notes SolidStats failed to copy estesis's "reviewer = pure delegation" discipline; with one canonical doctrine home, backend-ts, fetcher, and parser reviewers all cite the same [svc: §AA], instead of the parser reviewer citing a privately numbered translated section that structurally decays (the TS file grows §AC+, the mirror can't follow). On enforceability (criterion 8), the stated V2 con — "every rule written twice anyway" — overstates the cost asymmetry: the doctrine paragraph is the long, stable part; the per-stack evidence gate is one or two lines of grep-able idiom (`.catch(() => {})` in TS, `let _ =` on Result in Rust), and those gates must exist under EVERY variant for review to work — V2 just gives them a shared anchor to cite. On tokens (criterion 1), V2 explicitly permits keeping the thin shared TS translation layer, so the chain for server-2/fetcher work is the same depth as V1/V5 — the doctrine content is relocated out of the conventions skills (backend-ts-conventions is 16/29 ts-shared sections, the extraction pressure is measured), not added on top; the only genuine +1 read is parser tasks, where it buys closing the audit's #1 gap. V2 is also fully compatible with every hygiene win the other variants claim: utilities (es-toolkit/type-fest/day.js/nanoid, duplicated by commit db37f07 into backend AND frontend conventions, confirmed absent from ts-standards) still converge into process-ts-standards; TS test idioms still move up; V5's naming rule ("process- = meta layer, never direct-trigger, segment names the audience") can be codified verbatim. In short: V2 = V5's structure plus a canonical anchor above it, trading one small stack-free read for the only drift mechanism this corpus has ever seen work — and it is the only variant under which the question that started this debate has a one-sentence principled answer: "yes — the parser binds service doctrine; it does not bind TS idiom."

attacks.attack: V1 has no anti-drift mechanism at all — not even V5's note. Concrete scenario: during a server-2 task, §AB in process-backend-ts-standards gains a rule ('bounded channels must declare backpressure behavior'). parser-rust-conventions' one-time translated observability section is in a different repo-skill nobody is editing, with no marker linking it; parser-worker's lapin consumer never gets the rule. This is not hypothetical for this corpus: the same failure already happened with the severity table in backend-ts-code-review (CHANGELOG records the drift fix) and with the utilities block that commit db37f07 pasted into two conventions files instead of ts-standards. V1 also keeps 'backend' doing double duty (process-backend-ts-standards = two services; backend-ts-conventions = server-2 only), so an agent asked to write fetcher code plausibly reads backend-ts-conventions and follows its Fastify-shaped rules — the audit confirmed the existing 'fetcher baseline' note already under-describes exactly this mismatch (fetcher is pino/zod4/pg/commander/p-limit, no HTTP framework). And the trigger question gets answered 'no, by name construction' — i.e., the worker crate with lapin+S3+tracing, which shares every operational concern with the two TS services, shares zero written standards with them, leaving the audit's #1 gap closed only by a one-time translation with no maintenance story.

V2-lite moves only the six portable sections (SOLID, DRY, comments, portable code-quality bugs, lifecycle three-legs, swallowed-error) and leaves the actual service doctrine — §Z/§AA observability, config fail-fast, adapter taxonomy, graceful shutdown — TS-only. So it pays the new-skill cost without solving the problem that started the debate: corpus Gaps #1 (no Rust observability doctrine) is still closed by a V1/V5-style translated section with parity-by-note, the mechanism with three documented failures in this corpus. Worse, its cost line explicitly taxes EVERY stack including web — and web is a pre-code planning stub with no src/, so every future web task reads SOLID thresholds and rule-of-three doctrine that frontend-react-conventions will restate in React idiom anyway (the corpus shows frontend already restates delegated TS baseline 'despite delegation note', so the restatement is predictable). Concrete failure: an agent fixing a swallowed error in parser-worker now has two candidate homes for the rule — the new process-code-standards (portable half) and process-backend-ts-standards (service half) — plus the per-stack gate; doctrine fragmented across two files is strictly worse for lookup than one doctrine home or zero.

V3 re-creates the ~400-line shared band in two self-contained files (backend-ts-conventions and fetcher-ts-conventions) and bets on review discipline to keep them in parity. This corpus has already lost that bet at one-tenth the scale: the four-library utilities block was duplicated into backend and frontend conventions in a single commit (db37f07) instead of landing once in ts-standards, and the 19-agent auditor then MISREPORTED it as being in ts-standards until a hand check corrected it — if both authors and auditors misjudge where a 30-line duplicated block lives, two 400-line bands will silently diverge within months. Concrete scenario: the typed-error base gains a cause-chaining rule; it lands in backend-ts-conventions during server-2 work; fetcher-ts-conventions keeps the old form; the fetcher reviewer then approves code the backend reviewer would block — same product, same language, contradictory verdicts. V3 also openly contradicts the repo's own 'absorb once, single source' authoring standard, does nothing for the Rust observability gap, and leaves the parser question answered by vibes — failing judge criteria 3, 4, and 5 simultaneously.

V4 spends the largest mechanical churn of any variant (9+ skill renames: solidstats-server2-ts-*, solidstats-fetcher-ts-*, ...) on criterion 7 alone, and solves none of the audited findings: after the rename wave, the utilities duplication, the TS-test-idiom mislocation, the 400-line shared band, and the Rust observability gap are all exactly where they were. The corpus gives a precise preview of how the migration fails: AGENTS skill tables are ALREADY out of sync in all four repos for mere additions (project-standards and ts-standards installed+locked but missing from GSD:skills tables) — a rename multiplies that exact bookkeeping failure across skills-lock.json keys, four AGENTS tables, README, and the install state on every consumer machine. Concrete scenario: mid-migration, server-2's lock still references solidstats-backend-ts-conventions while the directory is now solidstats-server2-ts-conventions; the agent's install/lookup fails silently and it writes a Fastify route with no conventions loaded at all — a worse outcome than any naming ambiguity the rename was meant to cure. V4 is orthogonal to the actual problem; its one real benefit (scope words never lie) is available to V2 for free via V5-style naming rules in AGENTS, without breaking a single install key.

V5's entire anti-drift mechanism is a one-line note — 'mirrors §Z/§AA/§AB of process-backend-ts-standards — keep in sync' — and this corpus contains three documented cases of precisely that mechanism failing: (1) frontend-react-conventions/typescript.md restates no-any/no-interface/noUncheckedIndexedAccess 'despite delegation note'; (2) backend-ts-conventions' 'fetcher baseline' note that the audit found 'under-describes the mismatch'; (3) the backend reviewer's severity table, a consolidated second source of truth with a CHANGELOG-recorded unsatisfiable-instruction fix. Concrete scenario: §AA gains 'every retry loop logs attempt count and final disposition' during a fetcher task; no process fires on the parser-side mirror (no review skill checks cross-file parity — review-standards' scope discipline actually FORBIDS findings outside the change's scope, so a parser reviewer will never flag the stale mirror); parser-worker's lapin redelivery loop never gets the rule, and six months later 'mirrors' is false advertising — actively misleading, worse than no claim. The mirror also decays structurally: the TS file will grow TS-only sections (§AC+), so the section-letter correspondence the note promises cannot survive, and the parser reviewer can never cite the same § as the TS reviewers — the exact cross-stack review incoherence V5 claims to have answered 'principledly'. V5 is V2 minus the only working drift mechanism, purchased to save one stack-free read on parser tasks — the lowest-traffic save bought at the highest-risk spot (the repo with the confirmed gap).

own_weaknesses: Enforceability is genuinely idiom-level: any doctrine § that never gets its per-stack evidence gate written (e.g., the external-adapter taxonomy never gets a thiserror/tower-shaped Rust gate) is unenforceable dead weight — pure token tax that review skills cannot cite with a grep pattern. V2's value depends on the discipline of writing the thin gates, and the corpus shows discipline lapses are the norm here.

Highest read-chain of all variants for server-2 work if the thin shared TS layer is kept: project → ts-standards → service-doctrine → backend-ts translation → repo skill (5 deep) on the highest-traffic repo. The token cost is roughly relocated rather than added, but worst case (an agent that re-reads the whole chain per task instead of on-demand) makes V2 the most expensive variant exactly where most tasks happen.

Doctrine change fan-out: one doctrine edit still implies touching 2 idiom-gate files (TS + Rust); if the gates restate too much, V2 degrades into V3's multi-file edit problem with an extra file on top. The canonical anchor only helps if gates stay one-to-two lines.

No-code-samples doctrine is hard to author well: the worst case is vague principles ('be diagnosable') that fail judge criterion 8, or authors smuggling TS examples back in — recreating the original 'name says cross-stack, content says TS' problem one level higher. The parked draft must be split (6 universal vs 11 ts-shared sections), which is the largest authoring lift tonight of any variant except V4's rename wave.

Trigger precision risk: a stack-free 'service-standards' skill can mis-fire as a direct-use skill on coding tasks unless the V5-style 'process- = meta, never direct' rule is codified in AGENTS — V2 depends on borrowing that rule to pass criterion 2.

Audience boundary will reopen: 'service' cleanly excludes web today only because web is a pre-code stub; if web grows an SSR/BFF piece, the does-web-bind-service-doctrine question is the trigger question all over again with a different scope word.

Worst-case scenario overall: doctrine layer ships, Rust gates are half-written, and parser tasks pay a +1 read for doctrine the parser reviewer cannot enforce — i.e., V2 pays its costs in full and delivers V1's outcome.

advocates.strongest_case: V2-lite is the only variant that cuts the corpus along the seam the audit actually measured instead of a seam someone hoped exists. The 19-agent audit classified the draft layer (solidstats-process-backend-standards) as 6 universal sections vs 11 ts-shared — V2-lite moves exactly those 6 (SOLID thresholds, DRY rule-of-three, comments policy, the portable half of the code-quality bug list, the resource-lifecycle three-legs, the swallowed-error principle) into a slim process-code-standards and leaves the 11 TS-shared sections in process-backend-ts-standards exactly as V1/V5 would. Those six qualify for cross-stack extraction for a measurable reason: their evidence gates are already language-free — "~40 lines per function", "5 non-structural deps", ">3-branch dispatch on a union", "same logic 3+ times", "write path on a per-item path with no matching removal, TTL, or cap" — a reviewer can apply every one of them to a tokio worker, a React store, or a Fastify handler without translation, which dissolves V2's central con ("doctrine without idiom is unenforceable, so everything gets written twice") for precisely this subset and only this subset. The payoff is concrete on both gap repos. parser-rust-conventions has zero universal sections and no §AB analog (corpus gap #1), yet replay-parser-2 is a 5-crate long-lived tokio/lapin worker writing aws-sdk-s3 artifacts — exactly the "files/objects in a bucket never cleaned" and "module-level container that only grows" shapes the three-legs gate exists to catch; V2-lite delivers those gates to parser-rust-code-review via one require line instead of a hand-maintained translated mirror. web is a pre-code stub and frontend-react-conventions also has 0 universal sections, so under V2-lite the doctrine arrives before the first line of web code is written, rather than as a fourth copy retrofitted later. The drift mechanism is the decisive argument: this corpus contains two recorded failures of note-based parity — frontend's typescript.md restating no-any/no-interface "despite delegation note" (duplication #2), and the backend reviewer's severity table becoming a second source of truth with a CHANGELOG-recorded unsatisfiable-instruction fix (duplication #6) — while the require-graph mechanism (process-review-standards, process-testing-standards: cross-stack, single-source, 7 and 12 universal sections) shows zero drift findings in the same audit. V2-lite routes the six portable rules through the mechanism with the clean track record; V5 routes its most subtle content (the ~55-line three-legs gate with severity-escalation rules) through the mechanism with the failure record. Token cost is near-neutral where it matters: for server-2 and fetcher tasks the ~100 lines are moved out of process-backend-ts-standards, not added, so the TS read chain carries the same total; the only genuinely new reads are parser and web, where ~100 lines is cheaper than the V1/V5 alternative of a translated parser section of comparable size plus an eventual third statement for web. Update ergonomics follow directly: when the three-legs gate gets tuned after its first false positive in a fetcher review, V2-lite touches one file and all four reviewers inherit it; V5 touches the TS layer plus a parser mirror that nothing mechanical (no require, no lock entry) points at. Migration cost is a cut-and-move, not authoring: all six sections already exist tonight as separable headings (## SOLID, ## DRY — rule of three, ## §AB, ## Code-quality bugs, ## Comments & docs) in the parked draft's correctness-and-quality.md, and the AGENTS skill-table edits it needs in all four repos are edits gap #2 forces on every variant anyway. Finally, V2-lite inherits everything that makes V5 good — the process-prefix naming rule, utilities and TS test idioms converging into process-ts-standards (fixing duplications #1 and #5), the fetcher trio, backend narrowing to server-2 — so the trigger question gets the same clean answer ("the parser depends on shared doctrine, not on backend-ts"), but with the doctrine in a file the require-graph enforces instead of a sentence in a comment.

attacks.attack: V1 closes the Rust observability gap with a one-time translated §Z/§AA/§AB section inside parser-rust-conventions and provides no sync mechanism at all — not even V5's parity note. Concrete failure: the §AB evidence gate gets tuned after a false positive in a fetcher review (e.g. the 'ask rather than assume retention lives elsewhere' clause is strengthened after a reviewer wrongly flags a staging dir that the fetcher's run capability already cleans); the edit lands in process-backend-ts-standards, the Rust copy keeps the old stricter wording, and parser-rust-code-review — whose require chain (review-standards + parser-rust-conventions) never touches the TS layer — keeps emitting leak findings the TS reviewers would suppress. Same product, same leak shape, two verdicts, and no file relationship an editor can see. V1 also leaves web with literally nothing: frontend-react-conventions has 0 universal sections per the audit table, so when web src/ lands, a module-level Map keyed by replayId in a client store passes frontend-react-code-review because no skill in its chain contains the rule. And V1's own con admits the original trigger question survives: 'backend' still does double duty unless AGENTS spells it out — the naming problem that started this debate stays unsolved by structure.

The audit's stack-specificity table is the refutation of full V2: the draft layer is 6 universal vs 11 ts-shared sections, i.e. roughly two-thirds of the would-be process-service-standards is NOT stack-agnostic. To make it codeless doctrine you must strip the abstract-class AppError base, the as-const enum pattern, the Static<typeof X>/z.infer schema-first rule, envalid/Zod config — and then restate each in TS with its evidence gate anyway (the gates are idiom: 'no process.env outside the loader' is greppable, 'config fail-fast doctrine' is not), so all 11 sections get written twice, plus Rust translations the parser doesn't need (its error taxonomy is already thiserror-idiomatic; a doctrine § about 'typed error systems' adds nothing parser-rust-code-review can gate on). Concrete failure: a routine server-2 endpoint task now reads project-standards + service-standards + ts-standards + a thinned backend-ts layer + backend-ts-conventions — five reads, the deepest chain of any variant — and the doctrine file contributes zero greppable gates to the reviewer because every gate was pushed back down to idiom. Every doctrine edit then fans out to two or three translations, recreating at scale the exact second-source-of-truth drift the audit already documented in the backend reviewer's severity table.

V3 institutionalizes the failure mode the corpus already caught in the wild: commit db37f07 added the es-toolkit/type-fest/day.js/nanoid guidance to backend-ts-conventions and frontend-react-conventions simultaneously, and it is now duplication finding #1 — that is what 'self-contained per-repo skills' produces, observed, in this repo, within days. V3 scales that to the ~400-line shared band. Concrete failure: the typed-error rule about details-vs-message gets clarified in backend-ts-conventions after a server-2 review dispute; fetcher's self-contained copy is forgotten (nothing requires, links, or locks them together); two months later the fetcher reviewer cites the stale wording, the developer pushes back quoting server-2's newer wording, and the review deadlocks with both sides quoting 'the conventions'. Every doctrine fix becomes a 2-3 file edit needing its own parity review. It also flatly contradicts the repo's stated 'absorb once, single source' authoring standard, so adopting V3 means rewriting AGENTS.md's own rules to permit the duplication — failing judge criterion 7 by construction, not by accident.

V4 renames 9+ skills (solidstats-backend-ts-* → solidstats-server2-ts-*, etc.) in a corpus where the bookkeeping is already broken: gap #2 shows the AGENTS skill tables are out of sync in all four repos today, with only 14 skills and zero renames. V4 multiplies that surface — every skills-lock.json key, every GSD:skills table row, the README, and the literal hard-require lines inside backend-ts-code-review and backend-ts-tests (which name solidstats-backend-ts-conventions as a string) must change atomically across five repos. Concrete failure: the rename lands in the skills repo but server-2's lock still pins the old key; the next server-2 task resolves no conventions skill, and code review runs silently without the ruleset — the worst possible failure for a system whose whole job is making reviews cite sections. And the payoff is purely cosmetic: V5/V2-lite kill the 'backend' ambiguity with a one-sentence naming rule in AGENTS at zero rename cost, while V4 fixes none of the actual findings — the Rust §AB gap, the utilities duplication, and the TS-test-idiom misplacement all survive a V4 migration untouched.

V5 is V2-lite minus the doctrine file, and the delta is exactly its weakest part: parity-by-note. This corpus has already run that experiment twice and it failed twice — frontend-react-conventions/typescript.md restates no-any/no-interface 'despite delegation note' (duplication #2), and backend-ts-code-review's severity table became a second source of truth severe enough that the CHANGELOG records an unsatisfiable-instruction fix (duplication #6). V5 now proposes a third 'mirrors §Z/§AA/§AB — keep in sync' note guarding the most subtle content in the corpus: the ~55-line three-legs gate with its 🟠-default/🔴-escalation severity rules. Concrete failure: review-feedback tunes §AB's severity defaults in process-backend-ts-standards; the parser's mirrored section sits behind a one-line comment that no require edge, no lock entry, and no grep over the require-graph will surface; parser reviews systematically over-flag for months, and the person editing the TS file has no mechanical reason to know the Rust mirror exists. V5 also answers 'does web get SOLID/DRY/resource-lifecycle?' with 'no' — process-backend-ts-standards binds only the two services, no parity note targets React, so the six portable rules reach web only as a future fourth restatement, recreating duplication #1's pattern on the day web code starts.

own_weaknesses: Chain depth grows for the two currently-lightest families: parser tasks go from an effectively self-contained parser-rust-conventions (requires: none today) to a 2-3 skill chain, and web inherits a doctrine read before it has a single src/ file. On high-frequency small tasks (a CSS tweak in web, a clap flag in parser-cli) the ~100-line process-code-standards read is pure token overhead — V2-lite is worst exactly where V3's 'one read per task' is best.

No mechanical guard against scope creep: the boundary rule ('only sections whose evidence gates are language-agnostic') is an authoring convention, not a structure. The next contributor who thinks 'config fail-fast is doctrine too' can regrow process-code-standards into V2's full pyramid one section at a time, and nothing but review discipline stops them — the same discipline V2-lite criticizes V5 for relying on.

The split point inside the code-quality bug list is genuinely fuzzy and creates a two-file lookup: the portable half (empty catch, identical branches, sleep-as-synchronization, TODO-without-ref) moves up while 'no any', 'no console.*', and the never-assertion exhaustiveness rule stay TS-side — a reviewer wanting the full bug list now reads two files, and the split can be mis-drawn (e.g. 'no console.* — use the injected logger' is portable in spirit to Rust's println!-vs-tracing but idiom-named, so it could land in either home and drift between them).

It does not fully close the Rust observability gap and could create false confidence that it does: §Z log hygiene and most of §AA (field correlation by jobId/replayId, structured-field discipline) remain TS-idiom and still need a hand-written tracing-spans section in parser-rust-conventions. V2-lite only shrinks the translation debt to the non-portable remainder; the V1/V5 criticism ('doctrine exists in two written forms that can drift') still applies to that remainder at reduced size.

Largest migration bookkeeping of the non-rename variants: one new skill means new entries in skills-lock.json, new GSD:skills table rows in all four repos (which are already out of sync per gap #2), and a new hard-require line added to four-plus conventions skills, including giving parser-rust-conventions its first-ever require edge. Each touchpoint is small but the failure mode of missing one (a repo whose conventions skill silently never loads the doctrine) is the same silent-degradation V2-lite attacks V4 for.

The six-section classification rests on a single auditor's judgment, and the same audit already caught one auditor claim that was wrong (the utilities-already-in-ts-standards claim, corrected by hand). If even one of the six turns out to need per-stack qualification in practice (e.g. the ~40-line SRP threshold proving wrong for Rust match-heavy parser code, or the >3-branch OCP rule fighting idiomatic exhaustive match in parser-core), V2-lite must either water the rule down to vagueness for everyone or add per-stack exception notes — at which point that section has quietly become the two-home rule V2-lite exists to avoid.

advocates.variant: V3 — Self-contained per-repo conventions (no shared service layer)
advocates.strongest_case: The decisive fact in the audit is gap #3: replays-fetcher's real stack is pino, zod 4, pg, @aws-sdk/client-s3, p-limit, commander — no HTTP framework — and the auditor's verdict is explicit: "Fastify-shaped conventions genuinely don't fit; the 'shared baseline' note in backend-ts-conventions under-describes the mismatch." The famous "~400 shared lines" were extracted from solidstats-backend-ts-conventions, a file the audit shows is dominated by sections written in server-2 flavor (8 stack + 2 repo sections, Fastify/TypeBox/Kysely examples); to make them genuinely shared, every example must be rewritten stack-neutrally or doubled — which is the same authoring work as writing fetcher-ts-conventions self-contained, except the result is worse: abstract prose instead of evidence-gated idiom. Judge criterion 8 is the trump card: evidence gates need idiom (the variants doc concedes this itself in V2's con), so the only form of a rule a review skill can actually enforce is the per-repo form — under V3, that enforceable file is the *only* file, and a fetcher reviewer cites [conv: §X] sections containing pino fields, p-limit bounds and commander exit codes, not server-2 HTTP error-mapping prose the agent must mentally transpose. V3 also wins the hot path on criterion 1: skills are read hundreds of times per edit, and V3's chain for a fetcher task is project-standards → ts-standards → fetcher-ts-conventions (3 reads), versus 4 for V1/V5 — and the V5 "net tokens roughly equal" claim only holds for server-2, because for fetcher the shared layer is a superset read carrying the other service's sections. On criterion 2, trigger precision is trivially perfect: the original bug — "the name says yes, the content says no" for the parser — dissolves because no skill named "backend" exists above repo level; nothing for an agent to mis-fire on. Crucially, the corpus itself proves that the delegation discipline every shared-layer variant depends on already fails in this family: frontend-react-conventions restated the TS baseline "despite delegation note" (duplication finding #2), backend-ts-code-review's severity table is "a known second source of truth" with a CHANGELOG-recorded drift fix (finding #6), and commit db37f07 pasted the utilities block into two files in a single commit (finding #1). Three documented failures of pointer/note discipline — yet V1 and V5 propose more pointers and notes as the anti-drift mechanism. V3 is also what the corpus's own doctrine demands: "DRY rule-of-three" is literally one of the six universal sections in the parked solidstats-process-backend-standards draft, and the shared layer would have exactly two consumers (web is a pre-code stub, the parser is excluded by everyone) — extracting an abstraction layer at N=2, where one of the two has confirmed content mismatch, violates the rule the layer itself would preach. Divergence between the two services is partly a feature, not only a risk: fetcher's architecture is still converging (flat capability dirs — check/checkpoint/evidence/staging — vs server-2's modules/infra/operations layout), and a shared file couples both repos' rule evolution: a fetcher-motivated change must be vetted for server-2 impact before it can land. Update ergonomics (criterion 4) are nearly a wash anyway: under V5 a doctrine fix touches process-backend-ts-standards plus the parser-rust translation plus reviewer severity tables — 2-3 files — exactly V3's fan-out, because Rust always needs translation and reviewers always need gates; the pyramid saves at most one file per rare edit, bought with one extra read on every service task forever. Migration (criterion 6) is the cheapest of all variants with a shipped shared layer: abandon the parked draft (never installed anywhere — it's absent from every repo's require-graph except its own requires line), write fetcher-ts-conventions, move utilities to process-ts-standards (every variant does this), add the Rust §Z/§AA/§AB section (every variant needs this — V1 and V5 both require the identical translation work). No renames, no new lock entries in four repos, no new rows in AGENTS skill tables that are already out of sync in all four repos (gap #2), no new "process- semantics" doctrine to teach. V3 spends its budget on the one thing agents actually consume — a correct, local, enforceable conventions file per repo — instead of on taxonomy.

attacks.attack: Fetcher task: 'add retry with backoff to the S3 staging upload'. The agent's chain is project-standards → ts-standards → process-backend-ts-standards → fetcher-ts-conventions — four files — and file 3 is the band extracted from backend-ts-conventions, whose typed-error-base and external-adapter sections were authored in server-2 flavor (the audit counts 8 stack + 2 repo sections in the source file). The agent must transpose Fastify/Kysely-shaped examples onto pino/p-limit/@aws-sdk code, the exact mismatch gap #3 documents. The name still contains 'backend', so the original trigger bug survives in weakened form: an agent triaging a replay-parser-2 worker task ('the parser is also backend') still has to read or consciously reject process-backend-ts-standards. And V1's own con admits the doctrine exists in two written forms (TS + Rust) with no sync mechanism at all — so V1 carries V3's drift risk between forms plus the 4-deep chain V3 doesn't pay.

process-service-standards declares 'errors must not be silently discarded' with no code samples, binding server-2, fetcher, and the parser worker. Now parser-rust-code-review must enforce it: the evidence gate is `let _ = result`, `.ok()` discards, `unwrap_or_default()` masking — idiom that can only live in parser-rust-conventions. The TS reviewers need their own gate (empty catch, floating promise). One rule is now written three times: doctrine + Rust gate + TS gate; a doctrine edit fans out to N translations — the variants doc's own con, confirmed. Every service task in three repos pays +1 read for a file with zero enforceable content. The precedent argument collapses on the corpus's reference section: estesis, the mature family, has shared standards that 'own the contract... and know nothing about stacks' — review behavior is stack-free, code idiom is not. V2 invents a tier the reference architecture deliberately lacks.

A 15th skill (process-code-standards) holding six sections — SOLID thresholds, DRY rule-of-three, comments policy, half a bug list, resource-lifecycle legs, swallowed-error principle — becomes a hard read for all four stacks. First web component task ever written: the agent reads project-standards + ts-standards + process-code-standards + frontend-react-conventions, four files, to inherit a paragraph of rule-of-three prose. Operationally it adds a lock entry and an AGENTS table row in four repos whose skill tables are already out of sync in all four (gap #2: project-standards and ts-standards missing everywhere) — the family demonstrably cannot keep 14 skills' tables synced, and V2-lite grows the broken surface. Worst of all, splitting the code-quality bug list into a 'portable half' and per-stack halves means reviewers must stitch the list from two files — directly aggravating finding #6, where the backend reviewer's consolidated severity table is already a recorded drift surface with one CHANGELOG fix.

Rename 9+ skills to solidstats-server2-ts-*/fetcher-ts-*/parser-rust-*/web-react-*. Concrete breakage path: the skills-lock.json keys in four repos go stale; every hard-require line breaks (backend-ts-code-review and backend-ts-tests both require backend-ts-conventions — that's 6+ require edits across three families); AGENTS skill tables in all four repos must be rewritten while they are already out of sync (gap #2), and the README and any session memory referencing old slugs rot. And after all that churn the actual question — who consumes the shared band, and where does fetcher's content live — is still unanswered, because V4 is orthogonal cosmetics: it must still pick V1-or-V3 for the layer underneath. Largest mechanical migration of all variants, zero new enforceable content.

The parity contract is a one-line note in parser-rust-conventions: 'mirrors §Z/§AA/§AB of process-backend-ts-standards — keep in sync'. Scenario, three months in: someone tightens §AA in process-backend-ts-standards ('every retry logs attempt count and cause'). The reminder note lives in the file NOT being edited; the editor sees nothing, no reviewer reviews skill edits, the Rust side silently stays loose, and parser-rust-code-review keeps approving retries the TS reviewers would flag. This is not hypothetical — the corpus records this exact mechanism failing twice already: frontend-react-conventions restated the TS baseline 'despite delegation note' (finding #2), and db37f07 duplicated the utilities block into two files in one commit despite the single-source authoring standard. V5's anti-drift device is the device with a documented in-family failure rate, and it still pays V1's full bill: the 4-deep chain, the Fastify-flavored extraction shipped as 'shared', plus a new process-naming doctrine to teach across four repos with already-stale AGENTS tables.

own_weaknesses: A genuine cross-service doctrine fix (e.g., tightening the typed-error base or async-safety rule) is a hand-applied 2-file edit (backend-ts-conventions + fetcher-ts-conventions, 3 with parser-rust) with no mechanical parity check; if the editor forgets one file, the two TS services' review skills silently enforce different rules, and nothing in the family detects it — there is no review-feedback loop (gap #4) to hang a parity audit on.

V3 directly contradicts the repo's written 'absorb once, single source' authoring standard; adopting it requires amending AGENTS.md with a sanctioned-duplication carve-out, otherwise future skill-editing sessions will dutifully re-extract the shared band and undo the decision — agents follow the written standard, and the standard currently says V3 is wrong.

If web ships and a third TS service appears (or fetcher splits ingest from contract-checking), the shared band exists in three drifted copies and the extraction V3 deferred happens anyway — as a 3-way merge of diverged texts, strictly more expensive than extracting tonight from one source.

Writing fetcher-ts-conventions self-contained means authoring ~400 lines of doctrine in fetcher flavor against a repo whose architecture is still converging (the taxonomy doc itself says 'architecture when converged'); part of that prose is written against a moving target and will need rework, whereas a shared layer would have isolated repo-specific churn to a thinner file.

Cross-repo consistency that users actually observe — e.g., server-2 and fetcher sharing error envelope conventions or log-field names across the same pipeline — has no single normative home under V3; consistency depends on periodic manual diffing of two doctrine bands, a chore no one is assigned and the worst fit for this family's demonstrated table-sync hygiene (gap #2).

advocates.strongest_case: The current naming convention is already half repo-scoped, and V4 merely finishes the job: of the five scope words in skills/AGENTS.md (`backend, frontend, parser, infra, process`), `parser` IS the repo (replay-parser-2), `infra` IS the infrastructure repo, and `frontend` coincides with the single web repo — only `backend` is a genuine tier word, and it is precisely the word that spans three repos colloquially and produced tonight's trigger question. Under V4's own spec, `solidstats-parser-rust-*` keeps its exact current name; the fetcher trio does not exist yet and gets created fresh under the right name (V1/V5 create it too — and note V1's own tree already writes `fetcher-ts-conventions`, a repo-scoped name, proving every variant smuggles in repo scoping the moment two repos share a stack); the web repo is a pre-code stub, so renaming the frontend trio binds zero code; and the draft `process-backend-standards` is parked in the skills repo only, absent from every consumer lock. So the real marginal churn is 6 directory renames (backend trio + frontend trio), ~8 grep-verified cross-reference lines (ts-standards SKILL.md, README, review/testing-standards), and lock keys in server-2 and web — while replays-fetcher's lock, all four AGENTS skill-tables, and all installs must be rewritten under EVERY variant anyway, because the audit found the tables out of sync in all four repos and the fetcher must swap backend-ts-* for its new trio regardless. The "renames 9+ skills" con is therefore factually inflated, and today — pre-code web, nonexistent fetcher trio, parked draft, already-broken tables — is the cheapest moment this rename will ever be; every month of delay binds more planning docs and human memory to the wrong names. Against this near-zero marginal cost, V4 buys the only fix that operates where the failures actually happen. The naming lie is live in production today: replays-fetcher/AGENTS.md:151 tells agents that `solidstats-backend-ts-conventions` covers "любой роут, плагин, хук, схема валидации, дизайн эндпоинта — TS/Fastify backend" in a repo whose verified stack is pino/zod/pg/aws-sdk-s3/p-limit/commander with no HTTP framework at all. The V1/V5 alternative — fix the names' meaning by documentation — writes the disambiguation rule into skills/AGENTS.md, a file installed in zero consumer repos; at trigger time an agent sees only the slug and description, so under the corpus's codified "pushy descriptions / over-triggering is acceptable" standard, the scope word in the name is the last remaining precision lever, and V4 is the only variant that makes that lever truthful everywhere. The duplication evidence points the same direction: both confirmed duplications (utilities in commit db37f07, the restated TS baseline) were authored in the skills-repo maintainer view, where install-scoping gives no protection and the misfile target is chosen by name — "utility guidance for backend code → backend-ts-conventions" reads plausible under tier naming and reads obviously wrong as "tri-repo utility list → server2-ts-conventions". The mature reference family the audit holds up as the model already validates V4: estesis disambiguates same-stack repos in the slug itself (estesis-frontend-react-vc-code-review vs estesis-frontend-react-counterparty-code-review, backend-fastapi-vc vs backend-csharp-vc); when SolidStats hit the identical situation — two TS services on one stack — estesis's answer is a repo/product segment in the name, not a new tier word "backend-ts = the two services" that estesis never needed. Finally, V4 is the only variant under which the trigger question becomes unaskable rather than merely answerable: the parser worker (tokio, lapin, aws-sdk-s3 — colloquially the most "backend" component in the product) can never again be argued into a TS layer by name, because no skill is named "backend"; `process-*` tiers carry explicit audiences (all / all-TS / TS-services) and everything else carries its repo. V4 composes cleanly with V1/V5's content moves (utilities up to process-ts-standards, the TS-services shared layer, Rust §Z/§AA/§AB translation) — it is those structures with names that stop lying, purchased at a one-time mechanical cost the migration plan must mostly pay anyway.

attacks.attack: V1 institutionalizes 'backend' meaning two different things in one corpus: `backend-ts-conventions` = server-2 only, `process-backend-ts-standards` = server-2 + fetcher. Concrete failure: a maintainer adds a new shared TS-services rule (say, a retry/backoff policy for external adapters), greps the skills repo for 'backend', and lands it in `backend-ts-conventions` — which under V1 binds server-2 only — so the fetcher reviewer never enforces it and the two services drift exactly as commit db37f07 already demonstrated misfiling works (same author, same day, same content into two wrong homes). V1's claimed churn advantage is also smaller than advertised: replays-fetcher must uninstall all three `solidstats-backend-ts-*` lock entries and install the new fetcher trio anyway, and all four AGENTS tables must be rewritten per the audit's hygiene finding — V1 pays most of V4's migration bill and keeps the ambiguous names.

The audit's own table shows the draft layer is 6 universal vs 11 ts-shared sections — V2 erects a full cross-stack doctrine pyramid around a 35% minority of content. Concrete failure: `process-service-standards` declares 'no swallowed errors; every catch logs-or-rethrows with context'; the parser reviewer cannot gate on that sentence — it must state 'no `let _ = result;`, no `.ok()` discarding Err on fallible I/O, `tracing::error!` with fields', which lives in parser-rust-code-review regardless. So every enforceable rule is written twice (doctrine + per-stack gate), violating judge criterion 8, while replay-parser-2 — whose worker tasks today read 6 installed skills — gains a 7th mandatory read on every task. Update ergonomics invert: one graceful-shutdown doctrine change fans out to doctrine + 3 stack translations + 3 reviewer gates = 7 files.

V2-lite splits single doctrines across two tiers: 'resource-lifecycle three legs' goes portable into the new `process-code-standards` while §AB's TS form stays in the backend-ts layer — the same doctrine now has two homes that must be co-edited, recreating V5's parity problem while ADDING a read for every stack including web, a repo with no src/ directory. It also creates a third 'portable doctrine' home next to `process-project-standards` (which already owns the overlapping security minimums per audit finding #4) and `process-testing-standards`, with no decidable boundary — where does the comments policy or the swallowed-error principle live? Meta-skill trigger precision (criterion 2) degrades exactly where the corpus already has a documented overlap triangle.

V3's ~400 duplicated lines between server2 and fetcher conventions have a corpus-proven failure mode: the audit's finding #6 shows that even WITHIN one skill (backend-ts-code-review's severity table consolidated from conventions tags), a second source of truth drifted badly enough to require a CHANGELOG-recorded unsatisfiable-instruction fix. Concrete scenario: the typed-error base gains a `cause`-chain requirement; the edit lands in server-2's copy; the fetcher's self-contained copy keeps the old shape; the fetcher reviewer — citing its own copy — APPROVES code the server-2 reviewer would block, and the drift is invisible because each repo is self-consistent. V3 also directly violates the repo's codified authoring standard ('Absorb generic pattern-skills... single source'), so adopting it requires amending AGENTS.md to permit the very duplication the standard was written to forbid.

V5's parity contract is discipline-by-note, and the corpus already contains the experiment proving that discipline fails: commit db37f07 duplicated the utilities section into backend AND frontend conventions instead of ts-standards — same author, same day, with the 'single source' standard already written in AGENTS.md. A 'mirrors §Z/§AA/§AB — keep in sync' line inside parser-rust-conventions is weaker than that: the maintainer editing process-backend-ts-standards never opens the parser skill, and nothing fires in reverse. Worse, V5's codified naming rule literally assigns the same segment two meanings — `backend-ts` means 'the two TS services' in process- skills but 'server-2 only' in direct skills — and codifies it in skills/AGENTS.md, a file installed in zero consumer repos; the agent working in replay-parser-2's worker (tokio/lapin/aws-sdk-s3, colloquially backend) never sees the sentence that tells it `process-backend-ts-standards` excludes it. V5 answers the trigger question in a document the questioner never reads.

own_weaknesses: Repo-generation coupling: the workspace already contains sg-replay-parser AND replay-parser-2, and 'server-2' implies a retired server-1 — repos in this product get versioned and replaced. `solidstats-server2-ts-*` welds skill identity to a repo generation; when server-3 happens, the entire rename machinery (dirs, frontmatter, locks, tables, installs, cross-references) runs again, whereas tier names like 'backend' would have survived the swap untouched.

Most of the practical trigger-precision gain is already delivered by install scoping plus V1/V5's fetcher trio: within a consumer repo only that repo's skills are installed, so the fetcher agent physically cannot trigger server-2's renamed skill either way. V4's marginal precision gain concentrates in the skills-repo maintainer view and the shared-layer name — real (that is where db37f07 happened), but narrower than 'names never lie' sounds.

Rename execution risk: lock keys, computedHash values, and installed copies in BOTH .claude/skills and .agents/skills across four repos must move in lockstep; one missed lock key silently drops a reviewer skill from a repo and reviews run without the ruleset until someone notices.

V4 is orthogonal to the actual duplication findings: it does not by itself decide the utilities home, §Z/§AA/§AB ownership, or any anti-drift mechanism — it must bundle V1's or V5's content moves and inherits their parity weakness wholesale; judged purely on criterion 3 (duplication/drift mechanism), V4 contributes nothing.

History and grep degradation: server-2's .planning milestone docs, gsd-migration-journal entries, and prior commit messages (db37f07, 38fa132, f283fa0) all reference old names; cross-epoch greps and archaeology get permanently harder, and stale references in planning docs may mislead future agents.

AGENTS.md convention cost (criterion 7): the scope vocabulary {backend, frontend, parser, infra, process} must be formally redefined from tier-words to repo-words, every example in the convention rewritten, and 'server2' as a slug token puts a digit inside the scope segment — awkward to parse and a one-off exception to the otherwise word-shaped scopes.

advocates.strongest_case: V5 is the only variant that fixes every verified finding in corpus-audit.md while touching the fewest files, because most of it already exists on disk. The draft layer is sitting in the repo right now as solidstats-process-backend-standards/ (SKILL.md + references/correctness-and-quality.md), already written with exactly V5's shape: hard-required by per-stack skills, builds on process-ts-standards, owns the typed-error base, enums, config discipline, adapters, async safety, and §Z/§AA/§AB; its own description already says "Do NOT trigger this for an actual coding task". V5's migration is therefore a directory rename (adding the honest -ts-), one AGENTS paragraph, two content moves, and one new Rust section — versus V4's 9+ renames or V2's net-new doctrine skill. The extraction it preserves is empirically justified: the audit measured backend-ts-conventions at 16 ts-shared sections against 8 stack and 2 repo sections — the ~400-line shared band is the dominant content of that skill, and the fetcher's confirmed real stack (pino, zod 4, pg, @aws-sdk/client-s3, p-limit, commander, no HTTP framework) proves it cannot just consume the Fastify-shaped skill, so the band must live somewhere shared or be duplicated. V5 directly resolves both confirmed duplications: es-toolkit/type-fest/day.js/nanoid — added to two files in a single commit (db37f07) precisely because no single home existed, and hand-verified absent from ts-standards — converge into process-ts-standards, as do the TS test idioms (typed builders, test.each, @ts-expect-error, fake timers) currently stranded in backend-ts-tests but needed verbatim by fetcher tests. The naming rule is nearly free: AGENTS.md already contains the embryo ("the *-process-*-standards skills stay meta — read by other skills, not triggered directly"); V5 just generalizes it into one teachable sentence — process- means meta/shared, its target segment names the audience (ts = all TS repos, backend-ts = the two TS services, none = all repos) — which kills the trigger question permanently: the parser is not in any audience whose name it matches, by rule rather than by tribal knowledge. On the Rust observability gap, V5 is the only variant that closes it enforceably: the parser is a 5-crate tokio/lapin/tracing/thiserror workspace, where the doctrine's enforcement units are tracing spans, Drop/RAII, and bounded lapin channels — none of which a no-code-samples doctrine skill (V2) can gate; review skills need idiom-level evidence gates (judge criterion 8), so the Rust translation must be written inside parser-rust-conventions regardless of taxonomy, and V5 simply names the relationship with a "mirrors §Z/§AA/§AB — keep in sync" parity contract instead of pretending a third file prevents drift. Update ergonomics beat every alternative except V1: a doctrine change touches 2 files (TS layer + Rust mirror) versus V2's 3 (doctrine + 2 translations) and V3's 2-3 unmarked copies with no contract naming them. Token cost per task is a wash with today: process-backend-ts-standards replaces content that would otherwise sit inside backend-ts-conventions and fetcher-ts-conventions anyway, and the standards skills are read-on-demand references, not always-loaded prefixes. V5 also matches the proven estesis pattern the repo explicitly copied — shared standards own the contract, per-stack skills are thin, reviewers delegate — without importing estesis's mistake of stack-free files trying to bind stack-specific code. Finally, V5 fits the migration debt the audit found regardless of winner (AGENTS GSD:skills tables out of sync in all four repos, CI-pattern conflation): those fixes ride along in the same small migration, whereas V4 would multiply the very table-churn that is already broken. The honest summary: V1 is V5 minus the two cheapest safeguards (a one-sentence naming rule and a one-line parity note); every other variant pays strictly more — in reads (V2, V2-lite), in duplication (V3), or in mechanical churn (V4) — to answer a question V5 answers in a sentence.

attacks.attack: V1 is V5's structure with the safeguards deleted, and both deletions have concrete failure replays. (a) Naming: the shared layer is still called process-backend-ts-standards, and without the codified AGENTS rule ('process- = meta, target segment names the audience'), the original trigger question recurs verbatim — six months out, an agent on a replay-parser-2 worker-logging task sees 'backend' in the name, recalls that the parser worker is colloquially backend, and either reads 400 lines of TS idiom it cannot use or, worse, starts enforcing const-union-enum/ESLint rules on a Rust crate. The corpus shows this is not hypothetical: the whole debate started because the draft's name (process-backend-standards) said yes while the content said no. (b) Drift: V1 closes the Rust observability gap as a 'one-time translated section' with nothing naming the relationship. Next quarter a new §AA rule lands in the TS layer (say, mandatory correlation id on retry logs); the editor has no signal that parser-rust-conventions/references mirrors it, parser-rust-code-review never gains the gate, and the two services and the worker now log to the same pipeline with different diagnosability contracts. The repo already has documented proof this silent-second-source mode happens: the backend-ts-code-review severity table drifted and needed a CHANGELOG-recorded fix. V1 saves zero files versus V5 and buys both regressions.

V2 fails judge criterion 8 (enforceability) by construction, and the corpus shows the cost precisely. A no-code-samples process-service-standards cannot carry evidence gates: 'resource lifecycle' as doctrine is unenforceable, while the enforceable forms are idiom — pino child-logger fields and finally-blocks in server-2/fetcher, tracing spans, Drop/RAII and bounded lapin channels in the parser's 5-crate tokio workspace. So parser-rust-code-review and backend-ts-code-review still need the rules restated in their conventions skills; every doctrine rule is written THREE times (doctrine + TS idiom + Rust idiom) versus V5's two. Update fan-out worsens accordingly: one change to the swallowed-error principle = 3 files, with the doctrine file as a permanently-stale risk surface. Meanwhile every service task in three repos pays +1 hard-require read: a fetcher one-liner in staging/ now chains project-standards → ts-standards → service-standards → TS-translation layer → fetcher-conventions, five deep. Here is the concise brief with tagged lessons:

---

LAYERED CONVENTION/CONFIG SYSTEMS — TRANSFERABLE LESSONS

**TIER COUNT AND NAMING IN LINT/STYLE CONFIGS**

1. The practical ceiling for extends chains in real monorepos is 2–3 tiers: a shared-base package (e.g. `@org/tsconfig/base.json`), an environment-specialization layer (e.g. `react.json`, `node.json`), and a project-level override. Deeper chains add cognitive overhead without proportional benefit. [tsconfig Chaine Handbook / xjavascript.com]

2. The @rushstack pattern names tiers by runtime context, not strictness: `web-app`, `node`, `node-trusted-tool`. This is more durable than a generic `strict`/`loose` axis because the axis tracks real risk surface, not taste. [@rushstack/eslint-config npm]

3. ESLint's official shareable config convention is `eslint-config-<name>` (or `@scope/eslint-config`); the name should encode the audience, not the rule count. [ESLint Shareable Configs docs]

4. Microsoft Rush Stack uses a `-rig` suffix for tooling-config packages that bundle multiple configs and their dependencies together — a single install pulls the whole toolchain, preventing version-skew across projects. [rushstack/eslint npm]

5. In flat config (ESLint v9+), `defineConfig()` with `extends` flattens arrays automatically, enabling composition without manual spread. The ecosystem converged on 2 levels: a shared workspace package + per-project override. Anything deeper was identified as a pain point that prompted the `defineConfig` reintroduction. [ESLint blog 2025-03]

**ARRAY MERGE / OVERRIDE TRAPS IN EXTENDS CHAINS**

6. In tsconfig, `compilerOptions` scalars deep-merge (child wins); but `include`, `exclude`, and `files` arrays are fully overwritten — not merged. Projects that assumed merge semantics on `include` silently broke type coverage. This is a known footgun. [Medium: miyoon, TypeScript issue #42386]

7. Path-relative fields (`baseUrl`, `rootDir`, `outDir`) in a base tsconfig resolve relative to the file that defines them, not to the extending file. Any extends chain deeper than 1 level that uses path fields requires re-declaring them at each consuming level. [echobind post]

8. ESLint legacy `.eslintrc` chains had the same trap: extending `no-restricted-syntax` from a parent required copying the entire rule array into the child to add one entry — defeating the purpose of inheritance. Deep chains amplified this. [eslint/eslint issue #9192]

**DUPLICATION / COPY-PER-PROJECT FAILURE STORIES**

9. DefinitelyTyped's monorepo accumulated 2,247 separate `.eslintrc.json` files for 9,244 packages — a canonical example of copy-per-project duplication at scale. The per-file approach made global rule changes require mass PRs. [eslint/eslint issue #18385]

10. Path inheritance confusion in flat config caused root-level `ignores: ["scripts/**"]` to silently suppress `scripts/` directories inside child packages too. This class of bug (scope bleeding) is a direct consequence of nesting beyond 2 levels. [eslint/eslint issue #18385]

11. The `tsconfig-paths` library documented a case where `extends` was expected to deep-merge path aliases but only shallow-merged them, causing runtime module resolution failures. Teams that relied on inherited `paths` had to duplicate alias maps at every level. [tsconfig-paths issue #94]

**SKILLS / AGENT-SKILL ECOSYSTEM ORGANIZATION**

12. The SKILL.md open standard (originated by Anthropic, adopted at skills.sh) is a 3-layer progressive disclosure: YAML frontmatter (~100 tokens, always loaded) → SKILL.md body (loaded when triggered) → `references/` files (loaded on demand). Each tier costs tokens only when actually needed. [Anthropic skills repo / DeepWiki SKILL.md spec]

13. Anthropic's internal skill catalog, once cataloged, collapsed into ~9 functional clusters: library reference, incident runbooks, CI/CD automation, scaffolding templates, and similar. Clustering precedes naming — find the natural groups first, then assign names. [MindStudio blog / KDnuggets Anthropic guide]

14. skills.sh uses a project-overrides-user-overrides-system hierarchy (3 trust tiers). A lower-priority skill is shadowed but not deleted; this is the same "cascade" pattern as CSS. [Codex CLI Skills Ecosystem blog / inference.sh]

15. The `-ops` suffix convention (Anthropic internal) signals "comprehensive operational expertise for a domain" — design + implementation + operations bundled. The suffix encodes scope, not stack. [MindStudio blog]

16. 55% of all skills.sh entries are software-engineering workflows; web/retrieval skills get 5× more installs than code-generation skills. Taxonomy should reflect actual usage distribution, not idealized categories. [OSS Insight blog 2026]

17. The Agent Skills ecosystem deliberately keeps infrastructure thin: GitHub = storage/identity, CLI = package manager, directory = telemetry. Naming convention (`<topic>-rules.md`, `<topic>-definitions.md` for reference files) is enforced by the validator, not by folder structure. [agentskills.io spec / inference.sh blog]

**DESIGN-TOKEN TIER SYSTEM**

18. The canonical 3-tier model answers three distinct questions: primitives = "what values exist?" (raw, no meaning); semantics = "what are values for?" (intent + theming); component = "how does a component use them?". Applications should consume semantic tokens; primitives are an implementation detail. [Token Tier System Architecture — designsystemproblems.com]

19. Cross-platform parity is maintained by a build-time transformation pipeline (Style Dictionary being the reference implementation): tokens are stored once in platform-agnostic JSON/YAML, then transformed into CSS variables, Android XML, and Swift constants at build time. Drift is structurally impossible because there is no manual translation step. [Style Dictionary GitHub / Style Dictionary docs / door3.com]

20. Style Dictionary's "Deep Merge" phase detects property value collisions and emits warnings when a token is overwritten. Conflict detection is built into the pipeline, not left to code review. [Style Dictionary DeepWiki overview]

21. Material 3, Adobe Spectrum, and Microsoft Fluent are the three referenced exemplars: Material 3 for mode-aware semantic architecture; Spectrum for scale, localisation, and a11y tokenisation; Fluent for high-contrast and cross-platform mode-switching. All three commit to semantic tokens as the application-layer interface. [Design Systems Collective 2025]

22. Figma-to-code pipelines (Tokens Studio + Style Dictionary) enforce that the design tool and the codebase share the same token names. If a designer renames a token in Figma, the pipeline fails at build time rather than silently diverging at runtime. [Tokens Studio docs]

**SYNTHESIS**

23. Two tiers of shared config + one project-level override is the proven sweet spot across ESLint, tsconfig, and Prettier ecosystems. Adding a third shared tier requires a strong justification (e.g. separating runtime environment from strictness level).

24. Name tiers by what varies between them (runtime, domain, trust level), not by quality level (strict/loose). Quality-level naming ages poorly; context-level naming is durable.

25. Arrays never merge across extends levels in any system studied — they overwrite. Any layering design that relies on inherited arrays accumulating entries will fail.

26. Build-time transformation (Style Dictionary model) is structurally superior to convention-based parity: it collapses "keep N platform representations in sync" into a single source + N transforms, making drift a CI failure rather than a human error.

27. The 3-layer progressive disclosure in SKILL.md (frontmatter / body / references) is directly analogous to the primitive/semantic/component token tier: each layer is loaded only when needed, and the outer layer acts as a cheap index into the inner layers.

28. Copy-per-project duplication at scale (DefinitelyTyped's 2,247 files) is the canonical failure mode. The forcing function to centralize is always a cross-cutting change that requires touching every duplicate simultaneously.
